faq.answer: No. A diagnosis requires distress, impairment, duration, and appropriate assessment.
faq.question: Does weaker Gregariousness mean social anxiety?

faq.answer: Not necessarily. Medium, familiarity, purpose, and privacy can change preference.
faq.question: Are highly gregarious people equally active online?

faq.answer: Behavior and circumstances can change. This page does not forecast an individual score trajectory.
faq.question: Can Gregariousness change?

faq.answer: Yes. A preference is not an inability to do the opposite.
faq.question: Can highly gregarious people enjoy solitude?

faq.answer: Yes. Skill and desired amount of company are distinct.
faq.question: Can a socially skilled person have weaker Gregariousness?

sections.body:
Gregariousness concerns preference for being around groups and having frequent company. It describes desired social density—not social skill, popularity, loneliness, social anxiety, or inability to enjoy solitude.

“Gregariousness within Extraversion: preference for group company” is used on this page as a descriptive construct within the NEO/IPIP-NEO 30-facet framework. The official IPIP resource describes scales that measure constructs similar to NEO facets and lists item mappings ([S11](https://ipip.ori.org/Finding_Scales_to_Measure_Particular_Constructs.htm)); this does not make scores from different instruments, translations, or products interchangeable.

FermatMind has not published product-level reliability, validity, Chinese norms, or individual predictive evidence for the score discussed on this page. This material is for self-observation and education. It is not for clinical diagnosis, hiring screening, school admission, or replacing a career decision.

> **Content method and update:** FermatMind Editorial prepared this page with AI-assisted drafting and checked terminology, boundaries, and evidence against public personality-psychology sources. It is for self-understanding and education; it is not clinical diagnosis, hiring screening, or individual-outcome prediction. Substantive update: 2026-07-19; review mode: solo_operator; not clinically reviewed.
sections.heading: Evidence and Interpretation Boundaries

sections.body: A stronger tendency may seek gatherings and feel restored by shared presence. A weaker tendency may prefer one-to-one contact, small groups, or substantial time alone. Desire, skill, opportunity, and distress must be separated.
sections.heading: Precise Definition

sections.body: Gregariousness belongs to [Extraversion](/en/personality/big-five/extraversion), reflecting approach toward social company.
sections.heading: Parent Domain

sections.body:
- **Gregariousness versus Warmth:** [Warmth](/en/personality/big-five/facets/warmth) concerns friendly connection; Gregariousness concerns amount and group size.
- **Gregariousness versus social confidence:** Someone can skillfully manage a group without wanting frequent group contact.
- **Gregariousness versus social anxiety:** Anxiety involves distress and threat response. A preference for solitude is not a diagnosis.
sections.heading: Distinguishing Neighboring Facets

sections.body: Stronger Gregariousness may appear as seeking shared meals, group work, busy settings, and frequent plans. Weaker Gregariousness may appear as protecting alone time, preferring small interactions, or declining optional gatherings. Caregiving, remote work, access, disability, culture, and discrimination affect observed behavior.
sections.heading: Behavioral Cues

sections.body: Online groups may feel energizing to one person and draining to another. Familiar groups can differ from crowds of strangers. A socially demanding job may conceal a strong need for recovery after work.
sections.heading: Contextual Differences

sections.body:
- Inviting several people into an activity.
- Choosing lively shared environments.
- Processing experience through group conversation.
- Overbooking social time.
- Finding extended solitude under-stimulating.
sections.heading: Possible Expressions When Stronger

sections.body:
- Choosing one-to-one or small-group contact.
- Restoring attention through solitude.
- Limiting consecutive gatherings.
- Missing useful network contact when withdrawal becomes automatic.
- Participating fully when the group has a clear purpose.
sections.heading: Possible Expressions When Weaker

sections.body: Stronger Gregariousness can make group access and frequent coordination appealing. Possible costs include weak recovery time or crowding quieter collaborators. Weaker Gregariousness can support concentration and selective relationships; possible costs include reduced visibility or missed contact. Neither level ranks social competence.
sections.heading: Strengths and Costs

sections.body: A software lead enjoys a daily team room but schedules one quiet hour afterward. Group preference and deliberate recovery coexist.
sections.heading: An Original Case

sections.body: A polished conference host handles hundreds of attendees but spends the next day alone by choice. Public skill and role performance do not prove strong Gregariousness.
sections.heading: An Original Counterexample

sections.body:
1. Which group sizes feel inviting, neutral, or draining?
2. Does shared presence help even without conversation?
3. How much recovery follows a social event?
4. Are declined gatherings preference-based, fear-based, or resource-based?
5. Do online groups change the pattern?
sections.heading: Self-Observation Questions

sections.body: Compare one small-group activity, one one-to-one contact, and one equivalent period alone. Record anticipated and actual energy. The result is context data, not an anxiety assessment.
sections.heading: Low-Risk Action Experiment

sections.body: Return to [Extraversion](/en/personality/big-five/extraversion) or the [30-facet guide](/en/personality/big-five/facets). Continue with [Warmth](/en/personality/big-five/facets/warmth), [Assertiveness](/en/personality/big-five/facets/assertiveness), [Activity](/en/personality/big-five/facets/activity), [Excitement Seeking](/en/personality/big-five/facets/excitement-seeking), [Positive Emotions](/en/personality/big-five/facets/positive-emotions).
